catalog_quote: Every one of the few Tharti-Tharti words recorded by Jack Long was accented on the first syllable ... Tindale was as careful as always in noting accent when he wrote down data from the Yu-Yu speaker Bob McKinley in his ‘Murray River Notes’. There is not one single example of stress on the second syllable, but when we turn the page to the next note which is not from Bob McKinley but a note from Tindale to himself, we find the name of the main Murray River Ancestor Ngurúndari [fn. 28: Tindale always marks the accent immediately before the accented syllable, so he writes ‘Ngu"rundari’]: this name was and is well known all the way down the river. Going down the river from Yu-Yu to Ngayawang, there is no evidence on accents in the important work of Moorhouse and there are no initial consonant clusters. new_statements.quote: Tindale was as careful as always in noting accent when he wrote down data from the Yu-Yu speaker Bob McKinley in his ‘Murray River Notes’. There is not one single example of stress on the second syllable, but when we turn the page to the next note which is not from Bob McKinley but a note from Tindale to himself, we find the name of the main Murray River Ancestor Ngurúndari [fn. 28: Tindale always marks the accent immediately before the accented syllable, so he writes ‘Ngu"rundari’]: this name was and is well known all the way down the river. [...] The tendency to shift the accent to the second syllable when that began with a coronal consonant is therefore manifest only in the southernmost of the Murray River Languages.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accent-marked Yuyu data (Tindale's transcriptions of the speaker Bob McKinley) show no word stressed on the second syllable; in the authors' argument this means Yuyu, like the neighbouring Tharti-Tharti words 'accented on the first syllable', kept initial stress and did not share the Murray-mouth (Yaralde) shift of stress to a coronal-initial second syllable. Initial stress is the implicature of the passage, not an explicit rule statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Yu-Yu; the one second-syllable accent on the adjacent page, Ngurúndari (the Murray River Ancestor's name), is Tindale's own note, not McKinley's data.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, single-word transcriptions in a field notebook (one speaker, 1930s). The statement is a comparative aside in a grammar of the Mathi group (Victoria), made to test Goedemans' (1998) claim of an areal second-syllable stress shift along the Murray; it is not a phonological description of Yuyu.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog uppe1415 'Upper Riverland' = Yuyu / Yu-Yu [yxu] (AUSTLANG S19), with Ngawait/Ngawadj (S10), Erawirung/Yirawirung, Ngintait (S18) and Ngarkat treated as its dialects (Walsh; Wikipedia). The quoted statement concerns Tindale's data from the single speaker Bob McKinley, whom Hercus 1989:47 identifies as the speaker of 'Yuyu (Ngintait) from the Murray below Ned's Corner', i.e. the easternmost, Ngintait variety (no separate Glottolog code; AUSTLANG S18). Taplin 1879:29 confirms that the Overland Corner/Chowilla people 'call their language You-you'.
